newsitem.title: MEXICO: Pemex chief welcomes private petrochemical cash.
newsitem.headline: Pemex chief welcomes private petrochemical cash.

text.p: Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) chairman Adrian Lajous Friday praised the entry of private capital in the nation's state-owned petrochemical industry, saying the income will reinforce competitiveness after months of stagnation.

"The new companies can attract capital, have easier access to modern technology, enjoy greater operating flexibility and will contribute positively to the expansion of the entire industry," Lajous told a crowd of chemical company executives.
To ensure private investment in the nation's 61 petrochemical plants, a panel of executives called for fiscal incentives, reduced corruption and greater investor security.

"We need a 20-year policy to give investors security, rather than changing policies every sexenio," said Jaime Lomelin, director general of Penoles. Mexico's presidency changes hands in six-year terms known as sexenios.
During the eighteenth National Chemical Industry Forum, Lajous and chemical business leaders agreed privatization uncertainty and insufficient investment has dragged down the industry.
"We hope Pemex will invest its resources in more profitable areas to improve its activity," said Enrique Ochoa, director general of Grupo Industrial Resistol, subsidiary of Grupo Desc.
Earlier this month the government decided to sell a 49 percent stake of the nation's dominant petrochemical industry to private ownership.

As Mexico begins auctioning rights to different industries, from railroads to telecommunications to natural gas distribution, private investors have complained of changing plans and delays. Businessmen said they will review the latest petrochemical sale switch before committing capital.
Lajous also outlined the oil company's plans to recover from the more than 500 million square feet of natural gas production lost per day after the Cactus plant explosion three months ago.

By June 1997, Pemex plans to begin operations at a natural gas plant in its Nuevo Pemex complex, Lajous said. Total gas production should grow nine percent by the middle of next year compared with 1996, with a production of 3.86 million square feet of gas per day, he added.
Lajous said Pemex plans to produce an average 3.08 billion barrels of crude oil per day in 1997, a 7.8 percent increase from an estimated daily average in 1996 of 2.86 million barrels.
